summary:
starX is an interactive web app that turns NISAR radar data into evidence anyone can check. Its 3D globe is built from NISAR's real orbit data, and clicking any place on Earth shows every NISAR pass there and which of those passes can be checked against an optical image taken the same day.

For the Dancing with the SARs challenge we tracked surface change on the Gandak river in India using real NISAR L2 GCOV data. Between September and October 2026, 18 areas there got much darker on radar, which a typical flood map would read as new water. An independent satellite image shows all 18 were dry sand and fields, likely from harvest and drying soil, and our detector flagged none of them.

This matters because radar can darken for reasons that have nothing to do with water, and false flood alarms cost responders time. We also measured accuracy with a test we wrote down before seeing the data. On held-out areas of the Kosi River, NISAR open-water detection scored an F1 of 0.88, and our satellite geometry matches JPL's ISCE3 software to 0.12 mm.
details:
starX is a browser-based verification platform that tests whether surface changes detected in NISAR radar imagery are backed by independent optical evidence. Standard flood maps often treat any drop in radar backscatter as new water, yet radar responds to surface roughness and moisture—meaning a harvested field or exposed sandbar can darken just like flooded ground. Built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge, starX cross-checks NISAR observations against near-coincident optical imagery anywhere NISAR flies, identifies the most likely physical cause, and explicitly reports when evidence is insufficient to decide.

How It Works

  • Orbit View & Live Pass Finder: Visualizes NISAR’s 12-day repeat orbit on an interactive 3D globe anchored to real spacecraft ephemeris inside NISAR files. Clicking any point queries NASA’s CMR catalog live to list historical passes, predict upcoming overpasses, verify repeat-track timing (within 2 seconds at our study site), and identify pass pairs with cloud-free optical imagery within 24 hours.
  • Scene View: Displays real NISAR L2 GCOV radar data over the Gandak River in Bihar, India, complete with a guided walkthrough and a pixel-level inspector for every 90 m cell.
  • Evidence & Method Views: Presents every quality check as a mission-style GO / NO-GO status with exact measured values, alongside full processing steps, validation metrics, and known physical limitations.

Key Findings & Quantitative Accuracy

  • False-Alarm Elimination (Gandak River, Bihar): Between 12 Sep and 6 Oct 2026, 18 areas within our 242 km² study site darkened by at least 3 dB. A Sentinel-2 optical image acquired 18 hours before the second radar pass confirmed all 18 were dry land (exposed channel sandbars and harvested/drying fields). A naive "darker = flood" rule would have triggered 18 false alarms; starX’s calibrated threshold flagged 0 of 24,227 visibly dry cells.
  • Open-Water Validation (Kosi River): Pre-registering our rules before inspecting test data and tuning thresholds on half the map blocks, starX achieved F1 = 0.878 (95% CI: 0.80–0.90), MCC = 0.878, 96% precision, and 81% recall across 11,166 held-out cells (using Landsat imagery acquired 19 hours earlier)—vastly outperforming an unsupervised baseline (F1 = 0.22). Our orbital geometry matches JPL’s ISCE3 processor to within 0.12 mm in range.

Intended Impact & Benefits

  • Disaster Responders & Planners: Confirms whether a radar anomaly represents real flooding before deploying resources, reducing costly false alarms.
  • Global Accessibility & Education: Runs directly in any browser with zero login required, allowing anyone to check when NISAR will next image their region and enabling educators to demonstrate SAR physics interactively.

Why It Is Creative
In starX, verifiable evidence is the primary product: every claim carries its underlying quality check, and the system transparently flags NO-GO when conditions are inconclusive—mirroring a NASA launch readiness poll. Our automated pass finder also uncovered valid near-coincident optical/SAR pairs missed during manual search, while the 3D globe links orbital spacecraft telemetry directly down to a single 90 m ground cell.

Factors Considered

  • Geometric Comparability: Both radar acquisitions share identical track, frame, mode, and processing version, with viewing geometry differing by only 0.0002°.
  • Cloud Cover Rigor: Because September optical imagery over Gandak was too cloudy to verify new inundation, we strictly labeled that case "observed, not evaluated" rather than claiming unverified flood accuracy.
  • Class Imbalance: Because open water covered ~2% of Kosi cells, we evaluated with F1 and MCC rather than misleading raw accuracy (99.5%).
  • Physical & Calibration Limits: Accounts for provisional NISAR calibration status and optical inability to penetrate dense vegetation canopy.
  • Reproducibility & Security: Deterministic scripts regenerate every metric from recorded runs with file hashes, and zero credentials are exposed to the client browser.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Data

  • Languages & Libraries: Python (h5py, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, ISCE3, matplotlib, earthaccess) in the ASF NISAR Cookbook environment; JavaScript (Leaflet, globe.gl).
  • NASA & Partner Data: NASA CMR, ASF DAAC (NISAR L2 GCOV), LP DAAC (HLS / Sentinel-2 & Landsat), and NASA GIBS.
  • Hardware & Testing: Developed and verified on a MacBook across Chrome and Firefox using automated Playwright tests.
dataRefs: Xu (2006) MNDWI, Int. J. Remote Sensing 27(14)
